content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, 'belief' or 'to believe' (Greek pisteuō, Hebrew aman) is understood not as mere intellectual assent to facts but as personal trust in, reliance upon, and committed entrusting of oneself to God and to Jesus Christ, resulting in salvation and eternal life. It is the receptive act by which a person appropriates God's grace — trusting Christ's person and work rather than one's own merit. Classic theology unpacks it as three elements: notitia (knowledge of the content), assensus (assent that it is true), and fiducia (personal trust), with fiducia regarded as the decisive, saving element.","primary_basis":["John 3:16","John 1:12","John 20:31","John 6:29","Acts 16:31","Romans 4:3-5 (citing Genesis 15:6)","Romans 10:9-10","Ephesians 2:8-9","Habakkuk 2:4 (cited in Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, Hebrews 10:38)","Hebrews 11:1, 11:6","Genesis 15:6","Mark 1:15","Galatians 2:16"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Belief as intellectual assent alone (accepting propositions as true). Christian tradition generally treats this as insufficient by itself, citing James 2:19 ('even the demons believe—and shudder'), but some strands (e.g., certain 'free grace' teachers and popular usage) effectively reduce believing to assent to gospel facts.","basis":["James 2:19","John 11:27","1 John 5:1"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Belief as faithfulness, allegiance, or covenant loyalty — pistis rendered as ongoing fidelity and embodied allegiance to Jesus as King, not a one-time inward act. Associated with the Hebrew sense of 'emunah and with recent scholarship (e.g., Matthew Bates, 'Salvation by Allegiance Alone') and with New Perspective on Paul discussions.","basis":["Habakkuk 2:4","Romans 1:5 ('obedience of faith')","Romans 16:26","Galatians 5:6","Hebrews 11 (faith expressed in obedient action)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Belief as inseparable from works and obedience — faith completed and demonstrated by action, so that believing without corresponding works is dead. Emphasized in Catholic, Orthodox, and Arminian/Wesleyan traditions and in James; Protestants typically frame this as 'faith alone, but not a faith that is alone.'","basis":["James 2:14-26","Matthew 7:21","John 3:36 (believe/obey parallel)","Galatians 5:6"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Belief as itself a divine gift and effect of grace or election, not a purely human act — the Reformed/Augustinian emphasis that God grants faith.","basis":["Ephesians 2:8-9","Philippians 1:29","John 6:44, 6:65","Acts 13:48","2 Peter 1:1"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Belief as mystical union or abiding participation in Christ — Johannine emphasis where believing means coming to, feeding on, and abiding in Christ, stressed in sacramental and contemplative traditions.","basis":["John 6:35, 6:47-58","John 15:1-11","Galatians 2:20"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is a broad, recognizable consensus across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions that biblical 'believing' means saving trust/entrustment in God and in Christ, exceeding bare mental assent. The live disputes are secondary and concern emphasis: whether faith is best glossed as trust, allegiance/faithfulness, or gift; how faith relates to works (the James–Paul discussion); and whether faith is a one-time act or persevering disposition. These are debates within a settled core rather than competing symbolic meanings. The term is more a theological concept than a 'symbol' in the typological sense; interpreters treat it literally-theologically rather than allegorically."}
